symptom: a slowly swelling calf in a patient who had crushed that leg decades earlier
hook: an entire muscle had died and turned to a long slab of chalk inside the leg
whatYouSee: A long chalky mass fills one compartment of the calf with a bright rim and a darker middle and the bones beside it are untouched.
whyItMatters: Remote muscle injury can leave a calcified mass that mimics a tumour. Biopsy or surgery can cause infection and wound problems.
treatment: A typical stable lesion may be observed after specialist diagnosis. Uncertain or symptomatic masses need an individual treatment plan.
takeaway: Peripheral calcification in an old injured muscle compartment suggests calcific myonecrosis.

observations.expected: a large elongated calcified soft tissue mass filling one muscle compartment of the calf with dense sheet like calcification around its rim and a more lucent centre while the tibia and fibula stay normal
observations.observed: A large fusiform calcified soft-tissue mass is visible in the posterior compartment of the mid-lower leg on both projections, with a dense peripheral calcified rim and a heterogeneous but relatively less dense centre consistent with a more lucent core. The tibia and fibula are intact bilaterally with no cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or endosteal involvement. The mass fills one compartment and is extraskeletal.

observations.expected: The visible anatomy matches the requested AP and lateral lower leg including the calf soft tissues and the declared age and anatomical exceptions.
observations.observed: Two projections of the lower leg are shown: one AP and one lateral/oblique, both including the proximal tibia-fibula articulation and extending toward the ankle. Calf soft tissues are well demonstrated. The skeleton is skeletally mature with closed physes and adult cortical thickness, consistent with a patient over 60. No degenerative changes are mandatory and their absence is not flagged. Anatomy is coherent throughout.

findings: Two radiographic projections of the lower leg (tibia and fibula) are presented side by side, consistent with anteroposterior (AP) and lateral or oblique views of the same extremity
A large, well-defined ovoid soft-tissue mass is present in the posterior compartment of the mid to lower leg, interposed between the tibia and fibula, measuring several centimeters in long axis
The mass demonstrates heterogeneous internal calcification with a peripheral denser calcified rim and a central lobulated or popcorn-like calcific pattern
The adjacent tibial and fibular cortices appear intact without frank cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or endosteal scalloping identified
The bones otherwise show normal density, trabecular pattern, and alignment; knee and ankle joint spaces appear preserved at the margins of the images
The soft-tissue calcification is extraskeletal in location
differential: Extraskeletal (soft-tissue) chondroma or chondrosarcoma: the lobulated popcorn-type calcification pattern within a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass in the posterior compartment is characteristic of cartilaginous matrix mineralization
Synovial chondromatosis or extra-articular synovial chondromatosis: multiple calcified chondroid bodies forming a confluent mass could produce this appearance
Calcific myonecrosis: a fusiform calcified soft-tissue mass in the lower leg compartment with peripheral and internal calcification fits this entity, particularly given the compartmental location
anatomyConcerns: The right panel view is slightly oblique rather than a true lateral, making precise depth localization of the mass relative to individual muscle compartments less certain
Proximal femur and distal foot are not fully included, limiting full-length assessment of the extremity
No side markers (R/L) are visible in the provided image

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The combination of a large fusiform soft-tissue mass occupying a single posterior compartment of the lower leg, with a dense peripheral calcified rim and a more heterogeneous but less dense centre, in a patient with a remote crush injury and slowly enlarging calf swelling, is the hallmark pattern of calcific myonecrosis. This distinguishes it from extraskeletal chondroma (which is typically much smaller and not compartment-filling) and synovial chondromatosis (which is typically periarticular). The elongated, compartment-filling shape with sheet-like peripheral calcification and lucent centre is the key visible discriminator. The tibia and fibula are intact with no periosteal reaction or endosteal involvement, confirming extraskeletal origin. Both views (AP and lateral/oblique) show consistent geometry and attenuation of the mass. The obliquity of the second view does not undermine assessment. No side marker or lettering is present, consistent with requirements.
